Citation / study title: Adsorption properties of tetracycline onto graphene oxide: equilibrium, kinetic and thermodynamic studies
Material identity: Graphene oxide (GO) nanoparticles
Preparation/process reported: GO; source excerpt does not provide a full manufacturing cost or process inventory.
Experimental design and conditions: Isotherm tests: 2 mL GO suspension at 20 mg/L plus 4 mL TC solution (6–180 mg/L), pH 3.6, incubated overnight and centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 30 min; Methods and Fig. 6 specify 298, 303 and 308 K. Separate test protocols: general adsorption uses 25 mL TC solution in 50 mL flasks and pH 6–7; pH tests use 2 mL GO plus 4 mL TC at pH 2–10; kinetics use 2 mL GO plus 4 mL TC at pH 3.6. Do not transfer conditions across experiments.
Observed result(s): Kinetic equilibrium reported within 15 min under the separately described kinetic protocol. TC release/desorption up to 99.8% is reported in pH tests; it is not a repeated-cycle reuse metric. No directly observed qe value is being used here as the capacity endpoint.

Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors discuss π–π interaction, cation–π interactions and hydrophobic/dispersion effects; computational simulation also considered. Treat these as proposed/interpretive mechanisms, not directly measured force contributions.
Recovery / regeneration: Release/desorption investigated; release percentage up to 99.8% reported. No multi-cycle regeneration protocol was confirmed in the extracted sections.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No quantified cost, energy, synthesis yield or process inventory identified in the extracted article sections. Cost evidence: not established.

Publisher text checked 2026-10-30; DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0079254.

Material identity: Magnetic Fe3O4/reduced graphene oxide (rGO) composite; study compares Fe3O4@SiO2/rGO, hydrothermal Fe3O4/rGO (HT-Fe3O4/rGO), and co-precipitated Fe3O4/rGO (CP-Fe3O4/rGO). CP-Fe3O4/rGO showed best performance for both TCH and OFL. Abstract says co-precipitation; exact precursor ratios, detailed Fe3O4/rGO synthesis, reduction chemistry and yield unavailable in publisher preview. Hydrazine hydrate appears only as a general introduction example for GO reduction, not verified as the reagent used in this study.
Preparation/process reported: Primary ScienceDirect abstract/snippets: batch experiments varied initial concentration, adsorbent dose, excitation current, pH, coexisting ions and water-matrix components. Optimum TCH condition: C0=30 mg/L, dose=1.0 g/L, pH 5, excitation current 2 A. OFL optimum pH=7 under same stated concentration/dose/current. Contact time, temperature, RMF frequency, magnetic flux density, rotation speed, electrical power and energy consumption unavailable.
Experimental design and conditions: Abstract reports >96% removal for both TCH and OFL under the optimized FG-RMF conditions. TCH and OFL are distinct antibiotics; do not pool. Preview does not expose exact time-resolved or equilibrium qe values, nor a numeric TCH-specific qmax.
Observed result(s): Langmuir isotherms reported in abstract, but numerical qmax and fit statistics are not exposed in accessible publisher preview. Do not invent a capacity.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Pseudo-second-order kinetics reported; rate constants, qe and fit statistics unavailable in preview.
Kinetics / isotherm: Abstract reports FTIR-based π–π interactions and hydrogen bonding as dominant adsorption interactions. Finite-element simulations suggest RMF induces rotational motion of Fe3O4/rGO, increasing collision frequency and external mass transfer. Treat the field-driven explanation as authors' simulation/interpretation, not direct proof of energy efficiency.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Abstract reports >87% removal efficiency retained after four cycles. Regenerant, regeneration procedure and per-cycle numeric values unavailable. Distinguish retention of removal efficiency from capacity retention.
Recovery / regeneration: No power, energy, frequency or cost data accessible. RMF excitation current is 2 A, but current alone cannot establish energy consumption; no voltage, coil resistance, duty cycle or operating time reported. Complex-water performance is claimed, but matrix composition and exact results unavailable.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No power/energy or cost inventory. 2 A current alone is not energy consumption.
Source location within article: Official ScienceDirect primary publisher preview: abstract, introduction, Chemicals, Selection of adsorbent composite and Conclusion snippets. Metadata: Ning Ding, Luhui Xu, Yiyang Wang, Zixian Liu, Yang Zhan, Ran Zhao and Hong Liu; Separation and Purification Technology 382 (26 February 2026), article 136049; DOI 10.1016/j.seppur.2025.136049. Full text requires institutional access/purchase; full tables not accessed.
Extraction status: Primary ScienceDirect publisher abstract, introduction and section snippets rechecked 30 October 2026; no full Methods/tables accessed.
Caveats / next check: Keep TCH and OFL separate. Use >96% removal only with C0=30 mg/L, 1.0 g/L, TCH pH5/OFL pH7, RMF current 2 A; contact time and temperature unknown. No qmax available. RMF versus no-field enhancement is qualitatively shown across tested composite variants, but no numerical field-free control values or energy metrics accessible. >87% after four cycles is removal-efficiency retention; protocol unavailable. Do not claim low-cost or energy-efficient without power data.

Citation / study title: Decontamination of tetracycline by thiourea-dioxide-reduced magnetic graphene oxide: Effects of pH, ionic strength, and humic acid concentration
Material identity: Thiourea-dioxide-reduced magnetic graphene oxide (TDMGO)
Preparation/process reported: Primary publisher/PubMed abstract: TDMGO was prepared and characterized by SEM, TEM, EDS, TGA, FTIR, XPS, XRD and VSM. Detailed thiourea-dioxide reduction protocol, precursor ratios, Fe3O4 loading, washing/drying conditions, yield and reagent quantities are not available in the accessible abstract.
Experimental design and conditions: Aqueous TC adsorption study. Abstract confirms pH, initial TC concentration and temperature were investigated. It does not disclose exact batch volume, adsorbent dose, individual initial/equilibrium concentrations, contact time, agitation, separation or numerical ranges in the accessible abstract. The cited 1233 mg/g Langmuir q_m is stated at 313 K.
Observed result(s): Publisher/PubMed abstract reports a Langmuir maximum adsorption capacity q_m=1233 mg/g at 313 K. This is a fitted isotherm parameter, not a directly observed q_e. The abstract also reports that adsorption is only slightly affected by pH; NaCl facilitates TC adsorption with an optimum capacity when NaCl exceeds 0.001 M; increasing humic acid concentration slightly reduces adsorption.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Langmuir-fitted q_m=1233 mg/g at 313 K. Fit range, R², model parameter table, equilibrium concentrations and mass-balance conditions are not exposed in the abstract. Keep separate from directly measured q_e.
Kinetics / isotherm: Abstract states pseudo-second-order kinetics and Langmuir equilibrium model; no kinetic constants, experimental/fitted q_e values, fit statistics or concentration/dose ranges available in accessible record.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Abstract and keyword support chemical interaction/chemisorption interpretation; detailed molecular mechanism and evidence are not in the accessible abstract. Do not infer specific π–π, hydrogen-bond or electrostatic contributions without full text.
Recovery / regeneration: Abstract states the adsorbent could be regenerated and reused; number of cycles, regenerant, cycle-by-cycle removal/capacity and magnetic recovery details are not available in the accessible record.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No quantitative synthesis cost, product yield, energy inventory, recovery cost or cost per mass of TC removed in the accessible abstract.
Source location within article: Official ScienceDirect abstract and PubMed record; title/author metadata and DOI verified. Full Methods, result tables and SI not accessible in this audit.
Extraction status: Primary publisher/PubMed abstract cross-checked 30 October 2026; exact article identity and DOI resolved; full text/table-level parameters unavailable.
Caveats / next check: Use as a primary empirical TDMGO/TC study at abstract-evidence level. Report q_m=1233 mg/g only as an abstract-reported Langmuir-fitted parameter at 313 K; do not treat as measured q_e or rank against observed uptake. Exact concentration/dose/volume, isotherm fit statistics, detailed DOM/ionic-strength conditions and regeneration remain unverified. DOI is absent from inspected bibliography exports; no citation key assigned.

Citation / study title: Adsorptive Removal of Ciprofloxacin from Aqueous Media with Graphene based Composites
Material family: A — graphene oxide (GO); B — selected GO-bearing metal-oxide composite
Material identity: GO and GO–TiO2 nanocomposite. Standalone TiO2 is also tested as a non-core comparator and is not a review-family inclusion.
Preparation/process reported: GO: modified Hummers process using 3.0 g graphite, concentrated H2SO4 (volume not stated), 6.0 g NaNO3 and 12.0 g KMnO4; keep below 10°C for 4 h, then 4 h at 35°C; dilute with 300 mL DI water, add 15 mL 30% H2O2, wash to neutral, centrifuge 6000 rpm for 3 h, dry 70–80°C. GO–TiO2: 245 mL DI water +5 mL ethanol, pH adjusted with HNO3; Ti precursor from 15 mL ethanol +5 mL titanium tetraisopropoxide, heated 60–80°C; add GO 0.117 g, sonicate 30 min, dry at ambient temperature, grind and calcine at 450°C for 2 h (25°C/min). No yield or detailed cost/energy data.
Experimental design and conditions: Batch bottle method: 100 mL aqueous CIP solution, C0=10 mg/L unless otherwise stated; 150 rpm shaking; sample withdrawn at intervals, centrifuged 30,000 rpm for 3 min, supernatant measured by UV–Vis at 277 nm; triplicate experiments, reported deviation <10%; ambient temperature; pH unadjusted except pH tests. Kinetic dose series: GO 0.5–3 g/L; GO–TiO2 0.5–2 g/L; contact-time plots extend to 120 min. Abstract operating point: neutral pH, 1 g/L, 20 min.
Observed result(s): Fig. 4 reports at 20 min: GO removal 22%, 34%, 49%, 61% at 0.5, 1, 2, 3 g/L respectively; GO–TiO2 removal 24.5%, 31.5%, 41% at 0.5, 1, 2 g/L. At the abstract's 1 g/L condition: GO 34%, GO–TiO2 31.5%. The GO results and GO–TiO2 0.5/1 g/L values approximately reconcile with Table 1's source-labelled experimental qe when converted from removal using C0=10 mg/L and the stated dose. GO–TiO2 2 g/L does not: Fig. 4 gives 41% at 20 min (50.5% at 60 min), while Table 1 lists Exp qe=4.08 mg/g, implying 81.6% of the feed mass was removed at C0=10 mg/L and 2 g/L. Do not use that value.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Table 1 source-labelled experimental qe (mg/g): GO 4.41, 3.33, 2.47, 2.03 at 0.5, 1, 2, 3 g/L; GO–TiO2 4.84, 3.13, 4.08 at 0.5, 1, 2 g/L. These values numerically align with the 20-min removal series for GO and GO–TiO2 0.5/1 g/L, but the paper says equilibrium is reached near 20 min while Fig. 4 shows continuing uptake to later times (GO removal reaches 43–78% at 120 min). Treat the 'Exp qe' label as source terminology, not independently verified equilibrium qe. Table 2 Langmuir Q0 (fitted maximum parameter): GO 1.565 mg/g (R² .984); GO–TiO2 1.094 mg/g (R² .988). Freundlich fit is better (R² .997/.999); Freundlich Kf=124.4/1106.6 and n=1.322/.602. Kf is not qmax.
Kinetics / isotherm: Table 1 kinetic fits: text claims PFO best for both materials, but for GO at 1 and 2 g/L PSO R² (.988/.996) exceeds PFO (.984/.865); PFO R² is higher for GO at .5 and 3 g/L and for all tabulated GO–TiO2 doses. Fitted kinetic qe values are much lower than the source-labelled experimental qe values; keep model parameters distinct. Table 2: Freundlich has higher R² than Langmuir for both GO and GO–TiO2, consistent with authors' stated preference. Fig. 4 reports increasing removal with longer contact time, conflicting with the statement that equilibrium is reached by ~20 min.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors discuss boundary-layer and intraparticle diffusion, and pH-dependent CIP speciation. They attribute adsorption to surface area/functional groups and physico-/chemisorption in different passages; these are author interpretations, not direct mechanistic proof. A statement in §4.2 says GO–TiO2 can photocatalytically degrade CIP under UV–Vis radiation. The batch adsorption method does not describe deliberate UV irradiation during the adsorption step; do not count photocatalytic degradation as an adsorption endpoint.
Recovery / regeneration: No adsorption–desorption regeneration protocol or cycle-by-cycle reuse data reported.
Cost / feasibility evidence: Qualitative claims that GO is cost-effective/GO–TiO2 is economical are not a cost analysis. Hummers oxidation uses strong acid, nitrate, permanganate and peroxide with repeated washing/centrifugation; GO–TiO2 adds titanium alkoxide, ethanol, nitric acid, ultrasound and 450°C calcination. No reagent cost, yield, washing-water, energy, recovery or cost-per-mass-removed inventory.
Source location within article: Official IOP open-access proceedings PDF (13 pages; text parsed). Source pins: §3.1 synthesis; §3.2 batch method; §3.3 kinetics/conditions; §4.2 and Fig. 4 dose/time removal; Table 1 kinetic fits; §4.4 and Table 2 isotherms; §4.5 and Fig. 7 pH/concentration; §5 conclusions. A visual screenshot through the web PDF viewer was unavailable because the IOP PDF endpoint was inaccessible there; figures are reported only where the parsed text layer exposes values.
Extraction status: Primary open-access IOP conference-proceedings full text text-parsed 30 October 2026; official metadata and proceedings context verified.
Caveats / next check: Provisionally eligible by material (GO and GO–TiO2) and target (CIP), but low-confidence proceedings evidence. Use only condition-labelled removal values at 20 min, with the exact source caveats. Do not rank reported qe/qmax or kinetic fits. Keep GO–TiO2 2 g/L Table 1 qe quarantined; do not describe as a real-water study or count photocatalysis as adsorption. Publication is a conference proceedings paper, not a conventional full-length journal article.

Citation / study title: Sodium alginate/graphene oxide hydrogel beads as permeable reactive barrier material for the remediation of ciprofloxacin-contaminated groundwater
Material identity: Sodium alginate/graphene oxide hydrogel beads (GSA), designed as permeable reactive barrier (PRB) backfill material for ciprofloxacin-contaminated groundwater. The publisher abstract confirms the material and application; exact GO:alginate ratio, crosslinking recipe, bead size, washing/drying and product yield are not accessible.
Preparation/process reported: The primary abstract confirms synthesis of GSA beads and evaluation in batch adsorption and flow-through PRB columns. Detailed preparation parameters and reproducible synthesis quantities are not exposed in the retrieved publisher record.
Experimental design and conditions: Batch adsorption examined contact time, initial CPX concentration and ionic strength; the abstract says adsorption was not pH-sensitive. Flow-through columns examined flow rate, influent CPX concentration and ionic strength and were interpreted with a chemical non-equilibrium two-site model. Exact batch volume, dose, C0 series, temperature, agitation, column dimensions, flow rates and breakthrough data are unavailable in the preview.
Observed result(s): The publisher abstract reports a maximum adsorption capacity of 100 mg/g at pH 7.0. The abstract does not identify this as a directly observed qe or a specific fitted qmax; retain it as an abstract-reported maximum capacity.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: The abstract identifies pseudo-second-order kinetics and a Freundlich isotherm. An indexed ScienceDirect conclusion snippet reports equilibrium time of 72 h and later calls the same 100 mg/g maximum a Langmuir-model capacity. This conflicts with the Freundlich model attribution in the abstract and the preceding conclusion sentence; do not label the 100 mg/g value as a verified Langmuir qmax.
Kinetics / isotherm: Pseudo-second-order kinetics and Freundlich isotherm are reported in the abstract. The conclusion's separate Langmuir attribution for the 100 mg/g maximum creates a source-internal model-label inconsistency.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors propose hydrophobic interaction, electrostatic interaction, ion exchange, hydrogen bonding and pore filling. These are author-proposed mechanisms from abstract-level evidence; relative contributions were not independently quantified in this audit.
Recovery / regeneration: No adsorption–desorption regeneration cycle or adsorbent-reuse protocol is described in the accessible abstract/indexed snippets. PRB lifetime is an operational measure and must not be treated as batch adsorbent regeneration.
Cost / feasibility evidence: The article explicitly states that PRB lifetime and cost were calculated. Numerical cost/lifetime values, currency/year, assumptions, material quantities, replacement basis, system boundary and sensitivity analysis are not exposed in the accessible sources.
Source location within article: Official ScienceDirect publisher abstract/highlights; indexed Conclusions snippet (72 h equilibrium and separate Langmuir-model attribution); PubMed abstract cross-check. Full Methods, numerical column tables and PRB cost/lifetime calculation sections were not accessed.
Extraction status: Official ScienceDirect abstract, highlights and indexed conclusion snippets plus PubMed abstract cross-check rechecked 30 October 2026; full Methods, column tables and cost/lifetime calculations remain inaccessible in this audit.
Caveats / next check: Use as a groundwater/PRB application case, not as field-scale validation. Preserve the model attribution conflict: abstract says Freundlich and reports 100 mg/g at pH 7, while the indexed conclusion also attributes 100 mg/g to Langmuir. Keep 100 mg/g as an abstract-reported maximum with model attribution unresolved, not a verified qe or Langmuir qmax. The 72 h equilibrium time is reported in the indexed conclusion. Column dimensions, operating conditions, breakthrough values and numerical PRB cost/lifetime assumptions remain unavailable. No reuse-cycle evidence is visible.
